# Discussion

This study evaluated box-score player value indices against regularised adjusted plus-minus in nine EuroLeague seasons. PIR and a related composite depended strongly on player role, also among players with the same on-court impact, whereas RAPM did not; RAPM predicted future lineup performance better; and lineups selected by integer programming, whichever value they maximised, showed no detectable advantage over the five players coaches had used most.

The role dependence of box-score indices follows from their construction. Rebounds, blocks, high-percentage shots near the rim and fouls drawn are concentrated in interior roles, whereas perimeter contributions such as spacing the floor and moving the ball are only partly recorded in the box score. RAPM instead credits players with what happens to the score while they are on court, adjusted for teammates and opponents [@grassetti2020extended]. Four checks indicate that the difference is not an artefact of how roles were defined or of noise in RAPM: role effects on PIR remained when RAPM was held constant, when RAPM was corrected for measurement error with an instrumental-variable approach, when roles were defined without PIR components, and when the lower reliability of RAPM was taken into account. This agrees with evidence that simple efficiency indices weight scoring heavily and are not comparable across tactical roles [@senatore2022efficiency], that PIR's weights lack a formal justification [@carta2026winscore], and that alternative box-score indices can be more valid and reliable than PIR [@marmarinos2019structural]. In practice, PIR-type indices should not be used to compare players across roles, for example in scouting or contract decisions, without role-specific reference values [@courelibanez2025profiling].

The predictive comparison points in the same direction out of time but is inconclusive within seasons. Out of time, RAPM explained more of the variance in future lineup net rating than summed PIR or VAL, with confidence intervals for the differences that excluded zero. Within seasons, the slopes of RAPM-based lineup value and of first-half minutes excluded zero whereas those of box-score values did not, but in the subset in which all measures were defined none of the paired differences between measures was statistically distinguishable from zero. We therefore do not claim that RAPM, or any box-score index, adds information to the coach's allocation of minutes; this would require a joint model of value and minutes with greater precision than these data allow.

Optimised lineups showed no detectable advantage over the players coaches used most, and they shared about three of their five players with the coach's choice. Several factors can explain this. Coaches observe information that box scores do not record, including defence, matchups, health and practice performance, so their rotations already favour the best players; rotation structures themselves are associated with team success [@guo2022exploring]. Maximising estimated values selects players whose estimates are inflated by noise, so realised performance tends to fall short of the estimate — the optimiser's curse [@smith2006optimizer]; this would also be consistent with the point estimates, which favoured the coach five in most optimisation variants, although none of these differences was statistically significant. Finally, segment outcomes are noisy and optimised fives rarely play together exactly. Optimisation approaches to team building [@muniz2022sports] should therefore be evaluated against the coach's own choices; outperforming the team average is not sufficient evidence of added value.

## Limitations

All analyses relied on segment-level net rating, which is very noisy. The confidence intervals of the direct lineup comparisons spanned up to `{python} f"{max(v['GA95'][1] - v['GA95'][0] for v in DC.values()):.0f}"` points per 100 possessions, so moderate advantages or disadvantages of optimisation cannot be excluded; the result is an absence of evidence of benefit rather than evidence of equivalence, and no smallest worthwhile difference was specified in advance. Several measures, constraints and comparisons were examined without correction for multiplicity, which matters mainly for the isolated intervals that excluded zero. Interpreting role differences at equal RAPM as bias assumes that RAPM measures on-court impact equally well in all roles, which cannot be verified with these data; RAPM has itself been shown to depend on teammate quality and complementarities [@ghimire2020measuring], and alternative plus-minus formulations exist [@damoulaki2025lasso; @josephs2025hypergraph]. RAPM is itself estimated with error and penalisation and was used both as a value measure and to adjust for opponents; its out-of-time advantage, however, is judged against observed outcomes and does not presuppose that RAPM is correct. RAPM drew on all prior seasons, whereas first-half box-score values did not; box-score values pooled over the same period increased somewhat but their confidence intervals still included zero. Box-score values could not be computed for low-minute players; in the subset of segments in which all measures were defined, the RAPM slope was smaller and the minutes slope was no longer distinguishable from zero. In the out-of-time comparison the measures treated low-minute and unseen players differently (a replacement-level coefficient in RAPM, the mean value for box-score indices), which may favour RAPM. Role constraints in the optimisation used the previous season's role where available, but current-season roles for players new to the league (`{python} f"{100 * I['kisit_rolu_cari_sezondan_pay']:.0f}"`% of candidate players). The direct comparison excluded segments featuring both the optimised and the coach five and was possible only in team-seasons in which both were observed, which limits its precision; because coaches choose when to use each group of players, the two sets of segments may also differ in game state (for example, score margin or quarter), which was not adjusted for; rotation patterns in the EuroLeague depend strongly on game state [@sampaio2026beyond]. Lineup optimisation used season-half information and did not model fatigue, fouls or matchups, which coaches manage in real time. Finally, the results concern the EuroLeague; because data and code are open, they can be tested in other leagues.

## Conclusions

Box-score indices such as PIR rate interior roles higher than players with the same on-court impact in other roles, and lineups optimised on these or on plus-minus values showed no detectable advantage over coaches' own rotations. Clubs and analysts should not compare players across roles with PIR-type indices, and should evaluate any lineup decision tool against the coach's most-used players rather than against the team average.
